quiz.q: A flow has no error handling configured and an error occurs. What does the consumer get?
options: A generic response from Mule's default error handler — typically 500 with the error description as plain text
A structured JSON error defined in RAML
quiz.explain: If you do nothing, the default error handler is used; it doesn't know your requirement, so the response is unstructured.

quiz.q: Which component sends the final HTTP response, whether the flow succeeds or fails?
options: The HTTP Listener, using its Response or Error Response section
quiz.explain: The Listener's Responses tab has Response (success) and Error Response (error) sections, each with body, headers, status code and reason phrase.

quiz.q: What is the default body of the Listener's Error Response?
When does the error object exist in the Mule event?
options: Only when On Error Continue is used
Only after an error has been raised
quiz.explain: During successful processing the debugger shows no error object; it appears when an error occurs.

quiz.q: For the error type `HTTP:NOT_FOUND`, what does `error.errorType.identifier` return?
quiz.explain: The namespace is the part before the colon (`HTTP`); the identifier is the part after it (`NOT_FOUND`).

quiz.q: A DataWeave mapping does `null - 273.15`. Which error type is raised?
quiz.explain: The DataWeave expression failed inside Mule. A wrong city name (with 404 not in the success validator) gives `HTTP:NOT_FOUND`.

quiz.q: What does On Error Propagate do when the error type matches?
options: Ignores the error and continues the flow
Catches it, runs its inner components, then propagates the error to the next level (the Listener's Error Response)
Swallows the error and returns the success response
quiz.explain: It stops the process and propagates the error response to the next level; for a Listener flow, the Listener's Error Response is used.

quiz.q: To return `400 Bad Request` with a JSON body from an error handler, what do you configure?
options: Change the HTTP Request's response validator
Set payload plus `statusCode` and `reasonPhrase` variables in the handler, and map them in the Listener's Error Response
Set the Listener's Response section to 400
quiz.explain: Error Response: Body `payload`, Status code `vars.statusCode`, Reason phrase `vars.reasonPhrase`.

quiz.q: The only handler is for `HTTP:NOT_FOUND`, but a `MULE:EXPRESSION` error occurs before the HTTP Request. What did the response body show in class?
options: The original request payload `{"city": "Mumbai"}`, with default status code and reason phrase
quiz.explain: No handler matched, so the default handler ran; the Error Response body was `payload`, which was still the original request.

quiz.q: A wrong encrypted API key value makes `p('secure::…')` fail. Which status code did the class choose for this, and why?
options: 400 Bad Request — the client is at fault
404 Not Found — the key wasn't found
500 Internal Server Error — a mapping/decryption problem is on our side
quiz.explain: The decryption failed before the request was sent (`MULE:EXPRESSION`), which is a server-side problem.

quiz.q: Handlers are ordered: ANY, then HTTP:NOT_FOUND, then MULE:EXPRESSION. A NOT_FOUND error occurs. Which handler runs?
options: HTTP:NOT_FOUND, because it is more specific
ANY — handlers are checked top to bottom and the first match wins
quiz.explain: ANY matches everything, so the handlers below it are never reached. ANY must always be last.

quiz.q: When exposing APIs to external organizations, which error codes are generally used?
quiz.explain: Custom codes work only if both sides agree; for external consumers, standard HTTP status codes are used.

cards.back: There's one success response but many errors; telling the consumer the exact reason lets them fix their side or know it's ours.
Mule's built-in handling when none is configured — generic, plain-text `error.description`, typically 500.
Response: used on success. Error Response: used when an error reaches the Listener. Both have body, headers, status code, reason phrase.
Status code, e.g. `200`; reason phrase is its short description, e.g. `OK`.
Created only when an error is raised: `error.description`, `error.detailedDescription`, `error.errorType`.
Error raised when a DataWeave expression fails inside Mule (e.g. `null - 273.15`, or a failed `p('secure::…')`).
Raised when the HTTP Request target returns 404 and it isn't treated as success.
Error Handler, On Error Propagate, On Error Continue, Raise Error (Core → Error Handling); Try (Core → Scopes).
Catches a matching error type, runs its components, then propagates the error to the next level (the Listener's Error Response).

cards.front: Type and When on a handler
cards.back: Type matches an error type (select it from the list for the full `namespace:identifier`); When adds a condition.
In the handler set payload (JSON body) and vars `statusCode`, `reasonPhrase`; map them in the Listener's Error Response.
The consumer sent wrong data — client-side — so 400 Bad Request. No hard rule; the consumer must understand it.
4xx when the client sent something wrong; 5xx when the problem is on our side. Final choice is agreed with the consumer.
Goes to the default error handler; whatever payload is current may leak into the response.
Catch-all that matches every error — used for errors you didn't handle specifically.
Always **last**. Handlers are checked top to bottom and the first match wins.
Possible if consumer and provider agree; external APIs generally use standard HTTP status codes.
Right-click → Rename for clear names (e.g. `Error Logger`); remove the "Copy of" prefix after copying.
